# Which tuple orders mix?

Let $N=2^n$, let $T$ be the group of XOR translations, and let $G=\langle T,P\rangle$.
Each round applies the same fixed $P$ after a fresh shared uniform translation.
An order $t$ mixes when the output of every distinct ordered $t$-tuple converges
to the uniform distribution on such tuples. Throughout, a tuple order and the
number of rounds are separate parameters.

## An exact test for all tuple orders

Write $H$ for the normal closure of $T$ in $G$. Equivalently, $H$ is generated by
all $P^jTP^{-j}$, for integer $j$. The project’s block-of-rounds argument shows
that order $t$ mixes exactly when $H$ acts transitively on distinct ordered
$t$-tuples. Hornauer, Stephan and Wernsdorf already used normal fixed-length
round groups and double transitivity to study periodicity. Their Corollary 2
proves pairwise convergence for a Markov cipher whose round functions generate
the alternating or symmetric group. [Hornauer, Stephan and Wernsdorf, §2](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48285-7_41)

Given a truth table, **the full sequence of yes/no answers is computable in
time polynomial in $N$, even if $t$ is part of the input**. Furst, Hopcroft
and Luks gave polynomial-time permutation-group algorithms, including normal
closure. Apply them to the $n$ basis translations and $P$. Compute a
point-stabilizer chain for $H$. While the successive orbit lengths are
$N,N-1,N-2,\ldots$, each additional tuple entry can be sent to any remaining
point while fixing the preceding ones. The first short orbit determines the
first failing order. If one unused point remains, its image is forced, so
$(N-1)$-transitivity gives $N$-transitivity. This decision avoids the
$N(N-1)\cdots(N-t+1)$ tuple state space. Finding round-by-round distances is
a separate computation. [Furst–Hopcroft–Luks, FOCS 1980](https://ecommons.cornell.edu/entities/publication/f360d936-ad6c-47ab-8ceb-105c662e23d0)

The accompanying group classifier builds $H$ from successive conjugate layers
and exact Schreier–Sims membership tests. If one layer adds no generator, $P$
conjugates the generated finite subgroup into itself and therefore normalizes
it. The subgroup already contains $T$, so it is the required normal closure.
Each strict extension at least doubles the order. At most $\log_2(N!)$ strict
extensions occur, irrespective of the order of $P$. The optional SymPy
dependency is pinned in the script. [SymPy group operations](https://docs.sympy.org/latest/modules/combinatorics/perm_groups.html)

## The four-wise threshold

For $n\ge3$, **the following are equivalent**.

1. The walk mixes on ordered quadruples.
2. $G$ contains the alternating group $A_N$.
3. The walk mixes simultaneously on every tuple order $1\le t\le N-2$.

Every nonidentity translation swaps $N/2$ disjoint pairs. This is an even
number for $n\ge2$, so $H\le A_N$. If $G$ contains $A_N$, then $H$ is a
nontrivial normal subgroup of the simple group $A_N$, hence $H=A_N$.
An even permutation can realize any specified mapping on at most $N-2$
points because two unused images allow its parity to be chosen. Conversely,
a four-transitive $H$ of this degree must contain $A_N$ by the classification
of finite four-transitive groups. The proper exceptional groups have degrees
11, 12, 23 and 24. No power of two occurs. At orders $N-1$ and $N$, specifying
the ordered images determines the permutation, whose parity at round $r$ is
$\mathrm{sign}(P)^r$. Its total variation distance from uniform is then at
least $1/2$. For $n=1$ the two translations already constitute $S_2$, and
for $n=2$ every permutation is affine and $H=T$. [Cameron, Theorem 1 and classification commentary](https://cameroncounts.github.io/web/talks/14/wca1.pdf)

This is a corollary of the classification and the fixed-key-schedule group
criterion. It implies a threshold for *eventual* convergence. The numbers of
rounds needed for different tuple orders may still differ substantially.

## An explicit separation at orders two and three

Identify the bits with $m\ge3$ field coordinates over $F=\mathbb F_{2^b}$.
Thus $n=bm$. Use a cyclic coordinate rotation $R$ and the involution

$$Q(x)_0=x_0+x_1x_2,\qquad Q(x)_i=x_i\quad(i\ne0).$$

Set $P=QRQ$. In coordinates relabeled by $Q$, the translation normal closure
is exactly $\operatorname{ASL}(m,F)$, the affine transformations with
determinant-one linear part. Here is a direct proof.

- In these coordinates the round group is generated by $R$ and $QTQ$.
  Conjugating a translation with vector $u$ by $Q$ adds $u$ and changes
  coordinate zero by $u_1x_2+u_2x_1+u_1u_2$. All these maps are affine with
  determinant one. The rotation also has determinant one in characteristic two.
- Translations along coordinate zero commute with $Q$. Their conjugates under
  $R$ give all coordinate translations in the normal closure. Conjugating
  translation by $s e_2$ with $Q$ gives that translation followed by
  $E_{01}(s)$, which adds $s x_1$ to $x_0$. Thus the normal closure contains
  $E_{01}(s)$ for each field scalar $s$.
- Rotating yields the transvections along every adjacent pair around the
  coordinate cycle. For distinct indices their commutators give
  $[E_{ij}(s),E_{jk}(1)]=E_{ik}(s)$, up to the immaterial sign in characteristic
  two. Following a simple path around the cycle gives every $E_{ij}(s)$.
  Elementary row operations generate $\operatorname{SL}(m,F)$. Along with the
  translations, this proves equality.

Over $\mathbb F_2$, any two distinct nonzero vectors are linearly independent,
so, after translating the first point to zero, any ordered pair of remaining
differences can be sent to any other. This gives triple mixing. Four distinct
points with XOR sum zero stay affinely dependent in the $Q$ coordinates,
while affinely independent quadruples also exist. The largest mixing order
is **three**.

For $b>1$, $\operatorname{SL}(m,F)$ acts transitively on nonzero vectors,
giving pair mixing. There are now both collinear and noncollinear triples.
Collinearity survives every round in the $Q$ coordinates, so the largest
mixing order is **two**. The construction uses an established hidden affine
structure. The explicit cyclic construction and normal-closure computation
are project derivations whose priority remains unverified.
[Brunetta–Calderini–Sala on hidden sums](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2018.10.003)
· [Caranti–Dalla Volta–Sala on regular subgroups of affine groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0510166)

| Bits | Field coordinates | Computed order of $H$ | Largest mixing order |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 3 | Three over $\mathbb F_2$ | 1,344 | 3 |
| 4 | Four over $\mathbb F_2$ | 322,560 | 3 |
| 5 | Five over $\mathbb F_2$ | 319,979,520 | 3 |
| 6 | Three over $\mathbb F_4$ | 3,870,720 | 2 |

Reproduce the four-bit row with the following truth table.

```sh
uv run group_mixing.py 0 2 4 7 8 10 15 12 1 3 5 6 9 11 14 13
```

## A fast published certificate and a four-bit sample

A transitive group of degree $N$ containing a cycle of prime length
$N/2<p<N-2$ in the cycle decomposition of one element must contain $A_N$.
Indeed no nontrivial block system can admit this prime divisor, since the
block size and the number of blocks are at most $N/2$. A power of the element
isolates the $p$-cycle, and Jordan’s theorem applies to the resulting primitive
group. As $T$ is transitive, the classifier checks up to sixteen actual round
maps $P\tau_k$ for this certificate. Success proves **all** orders through
$N-2$ in one pass per key. Failure to find a certificate goes to the exact
group algorithm. Unger describes stronger cycle-type certificates and proves
that his Jordan and primitivity tests succeed on almost every uniform
permutation as the degree grows. His sample-from-a-group bounds assume
access to sufficiently random group elements. [Unger, Theorems 1, 9–11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.09431)

In the existing seeded four-bit sample of 10,000 tables, the classifier gave
maximum order **14 for 9,974** and **1 for 26**. The classic long-prime-cycle
certificate accounted for 9,437 of the 9,974 successes. The remaining 563
decisions used stabilizer chains. In particular, every observed pairwise
mixer also mixed on fourteen distinct inputs. The table in the preceding
section supplies a four-bit permutation with maximum order three that this
sample missed. The following command reproduces the audit from the repository root.

```sh
uv run --with sympy==1.14.0 python - <<'PY'
import csv
from collections import Counter
from group_mixing import group_profile

tallies = Counter()
with open("results/four_bit/samples.csv") as samples:
    for row in csv.DictReader(samples):
        result = group_profile(map(int, row["permutation"].split()))
        t = result["mixes_through"]
        assert (t >= 2) == (row["status"] == "mixing")
        tallies[t, "cycle_witness" in result] += 1
print(tallies)
PY
```

## Which algorithmic guarantees transfer?

- **Polynomial in table size, including variable tuple order.** Normal closure
  and stabilizer orbits give this bound without sampling. The implementation
  does not promise near-linear running time on every table. [Furst–Hopcroft–Luks](https://doi.org/10.1109/SFCS.1980.34)
- **Near-linear under a small-base hypothesis.** Babai, Cooperman, Finkelstein
  and Seress analyze Monte Carlo order and membership algorithms for small-base
  groups. The natural action of $A_N$ needs $N-2$ base points, so this
  hypothesis cannot support a uniform near-linear bound here.
  [Babai et al., ISSAC 1991](https://www.khoury.northeastern.edu/home/gene/papers/issac91.pdf)
- **Orbit sampling with a group-element oracle.** Lemmas 2.3–2.4 of the
  large-base reduction algorithm use nearly uniform independent group elements
  to sample point-stabilizer orbits. The cost explicitly includes generating
  such elements. A supplied $P$ table gives evaluations and actual generators.
  A universal cost bound for generating near-uniform elements of its
  translation normal closure would require another argument.
  [Large-base reduction, §2.2](https://doi.org/10.1112/S1461157000001236)
- **Primitivity tests.** Beals gives nearly linear bounds for broad classes
  when testing for block systems, with stated alternating-socle exceptions.
  A primitive group can still have several pair orbits. Primitivity alone
  does not settle the pairwise decision. [Beals, 2025 preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01884)
- **Typical random tables.** Łuczak–Pyber show that almost every permutation
  lies in no transitive groups except the two giants. Babai–Hayes address
  directly the group obtained by adjoining a random permutation to a fixed
  group. Eberhard–Ford–Koukoulopoulos sharpen estimates on permutations
  belonging to some proper transitive subgroup. These results already imply
  that one repeated uniform $P$ almost surely gives every order through $N-2$
  in the large-degree limit. Unger makes cycle-structure recognition
  constructive. None of those typical-input statements bounds the miss
  probability on each individual mixing table. [Łuczak–Pyber](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548300000869)
  · [Babai–Hayes](https://publi.math.unideb.hu/load_doc.php?p=1124&t=pap)
  · [Eberhard–Ford–Koukoulopoulos](https://doi.org/10.19086/da.849)

The references above establish several earlier routes to the same qualitative
decision. This review found no theorem among them giving the notebook’s full
near-linear, one-sided pairwise guarantee from **one fixed explicit table**
without extra hypotheses. That leaves the priority of the particular
Walsh-transform algorithm unverified.
